edges.effect_quant: In ASPREE, a randomized trial of 19,114 healthy older adults, 100 mg aspirin daily increased major hemorrhage versus placebo (HR 1.38, 95% CI 1.18 to 1.62). A secondary ASPREE analysis found intracranial bleeding also rose with aspirin (HR 1.38, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.84), and compliance-adjusted analyses suggested the bleeding penalty may be even larger than the intention-to-treat estimate.
edges.population: community-dwelling adults aged about 70 years and older without established cardiovascular disease who are considering low-dose aspirin for primary prevention
edges.mechanism: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase-1 and thromboxane A2 generation, reducing primary hemostasis for the lifespan of the platelet. In older adults with more fragile vasculature and higher baseline bleeding susceptibility, that antiplatelet effect more easily converts minor insults into clinically meaningful hemorrhage.
edges.summary: For primary prevention after age 75, the bleeding signal from low-dose aspirin is strong and consistent. The ASPREE program showed little cardiovascular upside in this population while repeatedly demonstrating more major or intracranial bleeding, making the net direction clearly harmful for bleeding risk.
edges.caveats: These findings apply to primary prevention in relatively healthy older adults and should not be copied over to people with clear secondary-prevention indications. Individual bleeding risk still varies with ulcer history, anticoagulants, uncontrolled hypertension, kidney disease, and frailty.
